metric.concurrency.normalization: 0-100 scale, 100 = best-in-class concurrency design (lightweight tasks + compile-time safety + rich library). Java scores highly for virtual threads plus mature library and memory model, short of perfect due to lack of compile-time race prevention.

raw_assessment.comparative_note: Java concurrency is now among the strongest in the fixed language set: virtual threads give Go-goroutine-like ergonomics while retaining a best-in-class concurrent library and rigorously specified memory model; lacks Rust's compile-time race freedom.
mechanisms: java.util.concurrent: mature library of thread pools (ExecutorService), concurrent collections (ConcurrentHashMap), synchronizers (CountDownLatch, Semaphore, CyclicBarrier), atomics, and locks (ReentrantLock, StampedLock)
Virtual threads (Project Loom, JEP 444, finalized JDK 21): lightweight JVM-managed user-mode threads scaling blocking code to millions of concurrent tasks without separate async/await syntax
Structured concurrency (JEP 480, preview) formalizes parent/child task lifetime and error propagation
java.util.concurrent.Flow and CompletableFuture give composable async pipelines
Memory model (JLS Chapter 17) is a well-specified happens-before model
synchronized keyword and monitor-based intrinsic locks as a simple built-in primitive
raw_assessment.sources_examined: JEP 444 (virtual threads), JEP 480 (structured concurrency), java.util.concurrent design, JLS Chapter 17 memory model; design-level assessment.
weaknesses: No compile-time data-race prevention comparable to Rust ownership/borrow checker and Send/Sync traits
Historical thread-per-request model was expensive before virtual threads (now mitigated)
No native async/await syntax; pre-Loom composition relied on callback-heavy CompletableFuture chains
Structured concurrency API still preview in most recent LTS releases

metric.ffi_interoperability_design.normalization: 0-100 scale, 100 = best-in-class zero-cost native interop with ergonomic safety (e.g., Rust/Zig extern C). Java's modern FFM API is a large safety-conscious upgrade over JNI but retains JVM-boundary overhead and manual layout descriptors, placing it upper-middle.

raw_assessment.comparative_note: Materially better than the legacy JNI baseline, but behind C/Rust/Zig zero-overhead direct ABI interop, roughly comparable to or slightly behind Swift/Kotlin given JVM boundary overhead and manual layout descriptors.
raw_assessment.mechanism: Java Foreign Function & Memory (FFM) API (JEP 454, finalized JDK 22), preceded by JNI for two decades
raw_assessment.sources_examined: JDK 22 FFM API (JEP 454) and java.lang.foreign package design knowledge; design-level metric, no execution required.
strengths: FFM API provides safe, arena-scoped native memory management (MemorySegment, Arena) without hand-written glue/native code, unlike JNI
Method handles + linker (Linker.nativeLinker()) allow calling C functions directly from pure Java via FunctionDescriptor, no C stubs required for simple calls
Confinement model ties native memory lifetime to Java thread/arena scope, giving compile-time-adjacent safety over manual malloc/free
jextract tool can auto-generate Java bindings from C headers, reducing boilerplate
Bidirectional interop: Java can expose upcalls via Linker.upcallStub
weaknesses: Legacy JNI (still widely used) requires hand-written C glue code and manual reference management, heavier than Rust extern C or Go cgo
FFM API still requires explicit layout descriptors mirroring C struct layouts by hand for complex structs; no automatic ABI struct derivation like Rust bindgen or C# P/Invoke source generators
No language-native unsafe-block syntax; native access flags are coarser-grained than Rust per-block unsafe
JVM/native boundary call overhead versus languages compiling directly to native code (C, Rust, Zig, Swift)
No first-class support for calling into other managed runtimes without native intermediaries
